seo.title: Darcy-Weisbach Calculator - Pipe Pressure Drop
seo.description: Darcy-Weisbach Pressure Drop Calculator — Calculate pressure drop in pipes using the Darcy-Weisbach equation with full parameter control with instant results & multiple unit support.

formula.explanation: ΔP = f × (L/D) × (ρv²/2). Friction factor f (dimensionless), L/D in m, ρ in kg/m³, v in m/s; /1000 for kPa.

content.introduction: The Darcy-Weisbach equation is the most accurate method for calculating pressure drop in pipes for all flow regimes. Requires an estimated Darcy friction factor (Moody chart or Colebrook equation).

example.description: 100m of 100mm pipe, f=0.02, water at 2m/s: ΔP = 40 kPa.

faq.q: How do I find the friction factor?
faq.a: Use the Moody chart or solve the Colebrook-White equation. For fully turbulent flow in commercial steel pipe, f ≈ 0.015-0.022.

faq.q: When should I use Darcy-Weisbach vs Hazen-Williams?
faq.a: Darcy-Weisbach works for all fluids and flow regimes. Hazen-Williams is only for water at typical temperatures and is simpler but less accurate.

The Swamee-Jain equation is an explicit formula for the Darcy friction factor: f = 0.25 / [log10(epsilon/(3.7D) + 5.74/Re^0.9)]^2. It approximates the Colebrook-White equation within 1% accuracy for Re > 5000 and is widely used in pipe flow calculations. Use this calculator for instant friction factor and pressure drop results.

faq.q: How do I convert pressure drop between bar and psi?
faq.a: 1 bar = 14.5038 psi = 100 kPa. For water, 1 m head ≈ 0.0981 bar. Convert using these factors when comparing results with pump curves or valve datasheets.

sections.heading: Unit Conversion for Darcy-Weisbach
sections.body:
**Pressure units**

- 1 bar = 100 kPa = 14.5038 psi
- 1 psi = 6.8948 kPa = 0.06895 bar
- 1 m water head ≈ 9.81 kPa ≈ 0.0981 bar

**Length units**

- 1 m = 3.28084 ft
- 1 inch = 25.4 mm

**Flow units**

- 1 m³/h = 0.2778 L/s = 4.403 US gpm

The Darcy-Weisbach equation ΔP = f × (L/D) × (ρV²/2) requires consistent SI units: length in m, velocity in m/s, density in kg/m³, giving pressure drop in Pa. Convert to bar or psi afterwards.
